questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Use a qualified language service and keep the safety plan out of the unapproved tool
choices.B: Remove the client's name and use the website because de-identification guarantees an accurate translation
choices.C: Use the website first and ask a family member to correct any mistakes later

questions.scenarioContext: An integrated-care counselor considers pasting a client's safety plan into a free AI translation website. The site retains submitted text, warns that translations may be inaccurate, and is not approved by the organization. Policy requires qualified language assistance for clinically significant communication.
questions.explanation: A safety plan requires accurate communication, and the organization's policy identifies qualified language assistance as the appropriate safeguard. Removing a name would not resolve retention, approval, or translation-reliability problems with the free tool.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Accept the friend's requests because bringing a support person grants access to future information
choices.B: Exclude the friend immediately without asking the client about preferences
choices.C: Speak directly with the client about the friend's desired role, privacy boundaries, and any specific permission before involving the friend

questions.scenarioContext: A client brings a close friend to intake for support. The friend begins answering every question and asks to receive appointment reminders and copies of future assessment results. The client has not yet stated what involvement is wanted.
questions.explanation: The client's invitation to attend does not automatically authorize ongoing disclosure or decision-making by the friend. The counselor should center the client, define the support role, and obtain specific permission for any future involvement.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Complete the most time-sensitive referrals first and explain the decisions afterward.
choices.B: Pause, acknowledge the loss of control, and present one option at a time while requesting consent before each next step.
choices.C: Ask the person to choose immediately from the full list so no service opportunity is missed.

questions.scenarioContext: An adult arrives at a crisis center after a sexual assault and becomes visibly overwhelmed as several available services are described. The person is medically stable and says, “Please stop deciding things for me.”
questions.explanation: A trauma-informed response reduces cognitive load and restores choice after an experience involving profound loss of control. Making referrals without consent or requiring an immediate decision from a long list would reproduce pressure rather than support stabilization.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Document Bao's uncertainty and coordinate qualified Vietnamese language support with the pharmacist or prescriber for the medication instructions
choices.B: Enter the instructions into a general translation application and explain the resulting directions to Bao
choices.C: Infer the dosing instruction from the picture on the label and tell Bao what it most likely means

questions.scenarioContext: Bao receives prescription instructions written in English but prefers health information in Vietnamese. He tells his counselor that he is unsure whether to take the medication with food. He has no acute symptoms, and an authorization permits communication with the pharmacy and prescriber.
questions.explanation: Medication directions should come from the dispensing or prescribing professional in a language Bao can understand. The counselor can document the access problem and coordinate qualified language support without interpreting the dose. A general translation application may produce unsafe ambiguity in medication instructions.

questions.prompt: Which intervention is the best fit?

choices.A: Ask the client to analyze what the hair pulling symbolizes before changing the behavior.
choices.B: Practice early urge awareness and a competing response that makes pulling difficult for a brief period.
choices.C: Recommend studying only in public settings where embarrassment will prevent the behavior.

questions.scenarioContext: A client who pulls hair when studying notices an urge only after reaching toward the scalp. The client wants a concrete behavioral skill and agrees to track the pattern.
questions.explanation: Awareness training and a competing response directly target the cue-behavior sequence and match the client’s request for a concrete method. Public embarrassment is not a therapeutic mechanism, and symbolic analysis does not teach an alternative response to the urge.

questions.prompt: Which process is most useful for creating an individualized professional development plan?

choices.A: Select the same annual courses as experienced colleagues regardless of current practice needs
choices.B: Choose training primarily in areas where the counselor already feels confident and successful
choices.C: Integrate self-assessment, client-population needs, outcome information, and feedback from qualified colleagues

questions.explanation: Multiple sources help identify gaps that confidence or habit may miss and connect learning goals to actual practice needs. Repeating colleagues' choices or studying only familiar strengths is unlikely to produce an individualized growth plan.

questions.prompt: What should the clinical director do?

choices.A: Finish sessions before evacuating so abrupt endings do not distress clients
choices.B: Search the building personally before deciding whether the threat is credible
choices.C: Activate the emergency plan, evacuate, contact responders, and account for clients and staff

questions.scenarioContext: During office hours, a caller makes a credible bomb threat against a counseling center. The center's written emergency plan requires immediate evacuation, a call to emergency services, and assembly at a designated location.
questions.explanation: A credible bomb threat requires immediate use of the center's established safety procedure. Delaying evacuation to finish sessions or having staff search the building would expose clients and employees to unnecessary danger.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate initial response?

choices.A: Restrict the employee's access, preserve the audit log, and report the event through the required review process
choices.B: Ask the employee to promise not to repeat the search and remove the event from the audit log
choices.C: Leave access unchanged until the neighbor confirms that the employee used the information outside the clinic

questions.scenarioContext: An electronic health record audit shows that a scheduling employee opened a neighbor's counseling chart despite having no work-related reason. The clinic's security policy requires immediate access control, preservation of audit evidence, and privacy-officer review.
questions.explanation: Access without a work purpose is a privacy and security event requiring containment and investigation under the stated policy. Preserving the audit evidence supports an accurate review, while waiting for proof of outside use leaves inappropriate access unaddressed.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is most consistent with this history?

choices.A: Bipolar I disorder
choices.B: Bipolar II disorder
choices.C: Persistent depressive disorder

questions.scenarioContext: A client has a history of a three-week major depressive episode. The client also reports a distinct five-day period of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, increased talkativeness, and unusual goal-directed activity that was observable to others but caused no marked impairment, psychosis, or hospitalization. There has never been a manic episode, and substances and medical causes have been ruled out.
questions.explanation: The history includes a major depressive episode and a distinct hypomanic episode without any manic episode. The absence of marked impairment, psychosis, or hospitalization during the elevated period supports hypomania rather than mania under the facts provided.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Follow the incident procedure immediately rather than waiting for evidence that the account was misused
choices.B: Delete the message and take no further action if the account still opens normally
choices.C: Send the suspicious link to coworkers so they can test whether it also accepts their credentials

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor enters credentials after clicking a convincing password-reset link and then notices the web address was not the clinic's domain. Security policy requires immediate incident reporting, password reset through a verified channel, session revocation, and device review.
questions.explanation: Entering credentials on the wrong site creates a credible compromise that requires prompt containment. Verified password reset, session revocation, reporting, and device review are safer than assuming normal account access proves that no intrusion occurred.

questions.prompt: Which intervention is most culturally responsive?

choices.A: Explore both commitments and help the student frame coping goals in a way that can support personal well-being and valued family relationships.
choices.B: Encourage the student to keep counseling secret so family attitudes do not interfere with treatment.
choices.C: Challenge family loyalty as a barrier to the independence needed for emotional health.

questions.scenarioContext: A first-generation college student says family members view counseling as selfish because personal problems should remain within the family. The student values family loyalty and also wants help managing stress.
questions.explanation: This response makes room for the student’s relational values and individual needs without treating them as mutually exclusive. Secrecy may intensify conflict, while labeling family loyalty as a barrier imposes an individualistic standard.

questions.prompt: Which content in a transfer summary most directly supports continuity with the next counselor?

choices.A: A chronological copy of every progress note, including material unrelated to current care
choices.B: Current goals, interventions and responses, important client preferences, and pending follow-up needs
choices.C: The diagnosis and appointment count without information about the client's current plan

questions.explanation: These elements tell the next counselor what is active, what has been tried, how the client responded, and what still requires attention. A complete note dump can bury the current plan in unrelated history. Diagnosis and visit count alone do not support an informed continuation of care.

questions.prompt: Which continuing education choice is most appropriate?

choices.A: Attend the center's marketing seminar because local availability makes its information most relevant
choices.B: Select evidence-focused education from qualified sources addressing current research, risks, limits, and counselor scope
choices.C: Avoid all learning about the topic because the counselor does not currently offer the service

questions.scenarioContext: Clients have begun asking a counselor about psychedelic-assisted counseling advertised by a new local center. The counselor does not provide this service and wants to respond from an informed professional position without claiming expertise.
questions.explanation: The counselor can become sufficiently informed to discuss the topic without claiming the ability to provide the service. Independent, evidence-focused education is more reliable than a local provider's marketing and more useful than avoiding an emerging topic clients are raising.

questions.prompt: Which initial planning response best supports collaboration?

choices.A: Establish an accessible transit goal with the client and schedule later review of the work concern
choices.B: Adopt return to work as the first goal because the spouse can describe daily functioning more easily
choices.C: Postpone goal setting until the client can communicate without supported methods

questions.scenarioContext: An adult in rehabilitation counseling after a stroke uses supported communication because of mild expressive aphasia. The client's spouse wants treatment to focus on returning to work, but the client consistently identifies independent bus travel as the immediate goal.
questions.explanation: The client has communicated a consistent immediate priority, and supported communication is a valid means of collaborative participation. Addressing transit first respects autonomy while leaving the spouse's concern available for later review rather than allowing it to replace the client's goal.

questions.prompt: Which counselor intervention best supports action?

choices.A: Ask the client to visualize the disadvantages of never receiving the benefit.
choices.B: Encourage the client to finish the entire application alone to strengthen self-efficacy.
choices.C: Develop an implementation intention specifying when, where, and how the client will begin with the friend’s support.

questions.scenarioContext: A client repeatedly plans to complete a benefits application but postpones it whenever the paperwork feels confusing. The client has identified a trusted friend who is available on Saturday morning and wants a concrete plan.
questions.explanation: An implementation intention turns a vague goal into a concrete cue-and-action plan and incorporates support the client has already chosen. Requiring solitary completion ignores the identified barrier, while visualizing consequences does not specify how action will start.

questions.prompt: What should the clinical director do?

choices.A: Postpone deployment until privacy, validation, disclosure, human oversight, service limits, and crisis procedures are established
choices.B: Deploy the bot only to established clients because the existing relationship supplies adequate oversight
choices.C: Deploy the bot with a disclaimer that the practice is not responsible for automated responses

questions.scenarioContext: A practice considers deploying a client-facing AI chatbot as a "24/7 counseling assistant." The vendor cannot explain how the bot handles crises, prevents fabricated advice, or protects conversation data. Clients would not initially be told that responses are automated.
questions.explanation: A client-facing tool labeled as a counseling assistant can directly affect care, privacy, and crisis response. A disclaimer or an established client relationship does not replace validation, clear disclosure, human accountability, and safe escalation procedures.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor handle informed consent?

choices.A: Have the sister sign immediately because an intellectual disability eliminates the client's ability to consent
choices.B: Ask the sister to leave and use the standard form without any communication adjustments
choices.C: Provide accessible explanations, assess the client's understanding and decision-making ability, and verify whether anyone has legal authority before involving a substitute decision-maker

questions.scenarioContext: An adult with a mild intellectual disability arrives with a sister, who says, “I always sign things for him.” No documentation identifies the sister as a legal decision-maker. The client communicates preferences clearly but needs extra time and simplified wording to understand written material.
questions.explanation: A diagnosis or support need does not by itself establish incapacity. The counselor should support the client's comprehension and assess actual decision-making ability while verifying, rather than assuming, the sister's authority.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor apply the intervention?

choices.A: Have the client repeatedly imagine the original nightmare without changing it until fear disappears.
choices.B: Help the client create a less distressing ending and rehearse the revised dream imagery while awake.
choices.C: Interpret each image as a symbol of an unresolved unconscious conflict.

questions.scenarioContext: A client has a recurring nightmare after a frightening event. The counselor is trained in imagery rehearsal, and the client is stable, interested in the method, and able to use imagery without becoming overwhelmed.
questions.explanation: Imagery rehearsal involves revising the nightmare script and repeatedly practicing the new imagery during waking hours. Replaying the unchanged nightmare is not the defining technique, and symbolic interpretation is not required for this intervention.

questions.prompt: Which mental status description best fits the client's thought process?

choices.A: Flight of ideas
choices.B: Circumstantial
choices.C: Thought blocking

questions.scenarioContext: When asked why work has become difficult, a client provides excessive detail about several coworkers and office routines. The information remains logically connected, and the client eventually answers the question after repeated redirection.
questions.explanation: Circumstantial thought includes excessive but logically connected detail before the person eventually reaches the point. Flight of ideas involves rapid shifts among topics, whereas thought blocking is an abrupt interruption in the train of thought.

questions.prompt: What is the counselor’s best response?

choices.A: Explain that counseling is collaborative, describe how the counselor and client may work together, and ask what kind of help the client expected.
choices.B: Reassure the client that the counselor will provide clear solutions once enough background information has been collected.
choices.C: Begin asking about symptoms because uncertainty usually decreases after the formal assessment is completed.

questions.scenarioContext: At an initial appointment, a client says, “I’m not sure what I’m supposed to do here. Are you going to tell me how to fix my life?”
questions.explanation: Clear orientation reduces uncertainty while inviting the client’s expectations and preferences into the working relationship. Promising solutions misrepresents counseling, and immediately shifting to assessment leaves the process question unanswered.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Delay disclosure because the order is personal information unless a client is harmed
choices.B: Give the required notice and ensure that compliant supervision is in place before continuing practice
choices.C: Arrange informal peer consultation without telling the employer about the board order

questions.scenarioContext: A board consent order permits a counselor to practice only with monthly supervision and requires written notice to the counselor's employer. The counselor has begun a new job but plans to wait until the employer asks about restrictions.
questions.explanation: A consent order is binding even if an employer has not asked about restrictions. Informal peer contact does not satisfy an explicit supervision condition, and concealment would compound the compliance problem.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do next?

choices.A: Collaboratively specify the experiment, the predicted outcome, and what observations the client will record.
choices.B: Assure the client that competent employees ask questions, making an experiment unnecessary.
choices.C: Ask the client to request help with the most consequential work task to produce a decisive result.

questions.scenarioContext: A client with perfectionistic beliefs predicts, “If I ask a coworker to clarify one instruction, everyone will think I’m incompetent.” The client agrees to test the prediction in a low-risk situation.
questions.explanation: A behavioral experiment is most informative when the prediction, test, and observable data are defined in advance. Reassurance asks the client to accept the counselor’s belief, while using a high-stakes task introduces unnecessary risk into an initial test.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Read every item aloud because using the same words preserves the validity of any standardized instrument
choices.B: Consult authoritative instrument guidance or an assessment specialist and use a supported accommodation or suitable alternative
choices.C: Administer the original visual form and interpret the results cautiously if the client misses any items

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor plans to use a visually presented career inventory with a client who has low vision. The counselor is trained in the inventory but does not know whether reading the items aloud would preserve standardization or whether an accessible form has been validated.
questions.explanation: An apparently simple change in administration can affect standardization and interpretation. Checking authoritative guidance and consulting when needed allow the counselor to select an accessible method whose use is supported rather than improvising an accommodation.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Use the agreed backup, confirm privacy, and continue or reschedule as appropriate
choices.B: Send a direct message through the client's public social-media account because it is immediately available
choices.C: Take no action because clients alone are responsible for restoring a failed connection

questions.scenarioContext: A routine telehealth session disconnects during discussion of a nonurgent work concern. The telehealth agreement designates a telephone call as the backup method and requires the counselor to reconfirm privacy before continuing.
questions.explanation: The advance agreement supplies a safe continuity procedure for a routine technology failure. The counselor should use that plan and recheck privacy rather than moving clinical communication to public social media or abandoning follow-up.

questions.prompt: What is the best preparation for the first post-discharge session?

choices.A: Adopt the discharge goal because the residential program had the most recent contact with Renee
choices.B: Review both records, note the difference, and prepare to ask Renee about her current goals and transition needs
choices.C: Disregard the discharge summary because the outpatient record established Renee's original preference

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor will meet Renee after she completes a six-week residential substance-use program. The discharge summary describes abstinence as the treatment goal, while the counselor's pre-admission notes document Renee's preference for a harm-reduction approach. No current outpatient goal has been confirmed.
questions.explanation: Both records contain relevant but time-bound information, and neither establishes Renee's present outpatient goal. Recognizing the difference prepares the counselor to clarify rather than assume. Automatically adopting or rejecting the discharge goal would place a record above Renee's current perspective.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate intake response?

choices.A: Refer the client elsewhere because prior missed appointments indicate poor readiness for counseling
choices.B: Explore scheduling and child-care barriers with the client and determine whether the agency's available supports make services workable
choices.C: Assign a standard daytime appointment so the counselor can evaluate commitment before discussing alternatives

questions.scenarioContext: A single parent who works rotating overnight shifts requests counseling at a community agency. The parent has missed appointments elsewhere because available times conflicted with work and child care. This agency offers some evening sessions and limited on-site child care.
questions.explanation: Intake should identify concrete access barriers and collaboratively evaluate whether available supports make participation feasible. Prior missed appointments under different conditions do not establish unwillingness, and imposing another unworkable time would not assess suitability.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Accept the case because general family counseling experience covers the required service
choices.B: Explain the limitation, refer to a qualified provider, and pursue specialized preparation only for future cases
choices.C: Begin services while reading the credentialing standards between sessions

questions.scenarioContext: A family court refers a parent and child for a specialized reunification service. The court's written order requires a provider with a particular reunification credential. A counselor has general family counseling experience but lacks that credential and specialized training.
questions.explanation: The required credential and the counselor's lack of specialized training make this service outside current competence. Preparation obtained prospectively may support later work, but reading standards while treating does not satisfy the present requirement.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor communicate to the social worker?

choices.A: Tasha's identified concerns and goals, along with any relevant coordination need permitted by the authorization
choices.B: Confirmation that Tasha has an anger problem because that was the stated reason for referral
choices.C: The complete intake narrative so the social worker can determine which account is more accurate

questions.scenarioContext: A primary care social worker referred Tasha for "anger management." During intake, Tasha describes caregiver strain and says her goals are to obtain respite and communicate more effectively with her father. Tasha has authorized the counselor to send the social worker a brief summary of engagement and goals, but not session notes.
questions.explanation: The authorized feedback should accurately represent Tasha's assessed concerns and client-defined goals. A referral label is not a confirmed clinical fact, particularly when the intake provides a different context. Sending the full intake would exceed the limited summary Tasha authorized.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor address this pattern?

choices.A: Provide more detailed health education so the client understands the consequences of nonadherence
choices.B: Identify and regulate the personal reaction, review it in supervision, and restore curiosity about the client's barriers
choices.C: Ask the medical provider to take over counseling because frustration means the alliance cannot be repaired

questions.scenarioContext: In an integrated care clinic, a client with diabetes has difficulty following a treatment plan. The counselor notices becoming irritated and lecturing the client, whose behavior reminds the counselor of a parent who rejected medical advice.
questions.explanation: The counselor's family experience is contributing to irritation and a lecturing stance. Recognizing and managing that countertransference creates room to understand the client's barriers instead of assuming that more information alone will change behavior.

questions.prompt: What should the intern and site do?

choices.A: Use the licensed title because the supervisor assumes responsibility for the intern's services
choices.B: Use the licensed title only with clients who already know the intern is a student
choices.C: Use an accurate intern title and clearly identify the qualified supervisor and supervised status

questions.scenarioContext: A graduate counseling intern is told to wear a badge reading "Licensed Professional Counselor" so clients will feel more confident. State law reserves that title for licensees, and the training site requires interns to identify their supervised status.
questions.explanation: The reserved title cannot be borrowed from a supervisor or used for selected clients. Accurate identification prevents misrepresentation and enables clients to understand the intern's training status and supervisory structure.

questions.prompt: How are client strengths used most effectively in a treatment plan?

choices.A: By documenting positive qualities separately from goals so they do not influence clinical decisions
choices.B: By translating demonstrated abilities and available supports into resources for attaining objectives
choices.C: By treating strengths as evidence that counseling barriers will resolve without specific planning

questions.explanation: Strengths become clinically useful when they are linked to specific goals, barriers, and action steps. Listing them separately or assuming they eliminate the need for planning does not show how they will support change.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor narrow the referral options?

choices.A: Recommend the closest program because distance is the most objective measure of access
choices.B: Compare the verified programs with Darius's stated criteria and let him choose among the feasible options
choices.C: Select a program based on which participant demographics seem most similar to Darius's background

questions.scenarioContext: Darius, a single father seeking help for gambling, wants a secular support group that he can reach by bus and attend while his child is in supervised care. The counselor has several recently verified programs in the referral directory.
questions.explanation: Referral fit depends on the combination of service approach, transportation, scheduling, and childcare that Darius identified. Comparing verified options preserves choice while screening out services he cannot realistically use. Geographic closeness alone does not address all of the access requirements.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor send?

choices.A: The entire file, including the separate notes, because the physician is involved in treatment
choices.B: The authorized relevant record, excluding separate notes unless specific authorization is obtained
choices.C: Only appointment dates because no clinical information may be shared with another treating professional

questions.scenarioContext: A client authorizes the clinic to send the client's medical record to a primary care physician for care coordination. The clinic maintains the counselor's private psychotherapy notes separately, and policy requires a distinct, specific authorization before those notes may be disclosed.
questions.explanation: The facts distinguish the general medical record from separately maintained psychotherapy notes and require separate permission for the latter. Care coordination does not erase that specific authorization requirement, but it also does not prohibit an appropriately scoped clinical release.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Avoid retaliation and base any care transition on clinical and ethical factors
choices.B: Make withdrawal of the complaint a condition of treatment because trust has been damaged
choices.C: End services immediately without referrals so the counselor does not influence the investigation

questions.scenarioContext: A current client files an ethics complaint against a counselor. The counselor is angry and considers stating that counseling will continue only if the client withdraws the complaint. The client has not threatened the counselor or disrupted sessions.
questions.explanation: Conditioning treatment on withdrawal would use the counseling relationship to pressure the complainant. Any decision about continued services should rest on clinical and ethical factors, with appropriate continuity planning rather than punishment or abrupt abandonment.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate intake action?

choices.A: Explain the clinic's scope, check for urgent concerns and interest in counseling, and offer an appropriate prescribing referral
choices.B: Schedule the person with a counselor and imply that the counselor can adjust medication after the first session
choices.C: Reject the request without assessing urgency or explaining available referral and counseling options

questions.scenarioContext: A person contacts a counseling-only clinic requesting evaluation and management of psychiatric medication. The clinic has no prescriber but can provide counseling and maintains referral relationships with medical providers.
questions.explanation: The clinic should accurately describe its nonprescribing role while determining whether urgent needs or counseling interests are present. A referral can address medication services without misrepresenting the counselor's scope or abruptly dismissing the person.

questions.prompt: What does a score on a criterion-referenced assessment primarily indicate?

choices.A: Performance in relation to defined knowledge or skill standards
choices.B: Rank compared with a representative norm group
choices.C: Consistency of scores across different raters

questions.explanation: Criterion-referenced scores indicate performance against specified objectives or standards. Norm-referenced scores instead describe standing relative to a comparison group.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor address the diagnosis in treatment planning?

choices.A: Avoid the term in future sessions so the client does not become discouraged by diagnostic language
choices.B: Emphasize that the diagnosis is correct and proceed with goals even if the client remains doubtful
choices.C: Clarify what the diagnosis describes, correct the permanence assumption, and invite questions while setting goals together

questions.scenarioContext: A client diagnosed with persistent depressive disorder says, “Persistent must mean permanent, so goals will not matter.” The client is considering ending counseling before the initial plan is completed.
questions.explanation: The client's misunderstanding is directly affecting willingness to plan treatment. Clear, collaborative review can distinguish a diagnostic course descriptor from a prediction that change is impossible and can restore informed participation.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Pay the requested amount personally so no insurance record is created
choices.B: Notify the carrier promptly, preserve the record, and follow appropriate legal and claims guidance
choices.C: Revise the record to add details that make the counselor's decisions appear more defensible

questions.scenarioContext: A former client sends a written demand alleging harm and requesting payment. The counselor's professional liability policy requires prompt notice of any potential claim and instructs the insured not to admit liability or alter records before receiving guidance.
questions.explanation: The written demand is a potential claim under the policy's stated notice term. Prompt reporting and record preservation protect the response process, whereas personal payment or retrospective record alteration could create additional professional and coverage problems.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor address confidentiality at intake?

choices.A: Promise complete confidentiality because the probation officer is not part of treatment
choices.B: Explain the mandated status and reporting limits, obtain informed consent, and disclose only the required information
choices.C: Tell the client that the complete record will be sent monthly because court involvement removes confidentiality

questions.scenarioContext: A client is ordered to attend counseling as a condition of probation. The order requires the counselor to report monthly attendance and whether the client participates, but it does not authorize disclosure of session content.
questions.explanation: A mandated client needs clear information about what will be reported, to whom, and why before counseling proceeds. The order authorizes attendance and participation reports, not unrestricted session content, so disclosure should remain within that boundary.

questions.prompt: What is the counselor's most appropriate response?

choices.A: Refer the couple immediately because personal-value conflicts always justify ending services
choices.B: Seek consultation to manage personal values and continue competent, nondiscriminatory counseling
choices.C: Explain the counselor's disapproval so the couple can decide whether to remain in counseling

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor realizes that personal beliefs are creating discomfort while working with a same-sex couple. The counselor is otherwise trained to address the couple's presenting concern, and no competence-based reason for referral exists.
questions.explanation: The counselor is competent to address the presenting concern, so personal discomfort alone is not a client-centered reason to refer. Consultation can help prevent value imposition and preserve equitable care without burdening the couple with the counselor's beliefs.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Extend the session until the client has fully discussed the issue, regardless of later appointments.
choices.B: Ask the client to wait until the next session because beginning a new topic near closing is inappropriate.
choices.C: Acknowledge the importance, clarify enough to support containment, and agree on how to return to it promptly.

questions.scenarioContext: With two minutes remaining, a client says, “There’s something important I haven’t told you about my marriage.” The client states there is no immediate safety concern but does not want the issue ignored.
questions.explanation: This response respects both the significance of the disclosure and the real session boundary. It avoids opening material that cannot be held adequately while ensuring the client does not experience the concern as dismissed.

questions.prompt: Which revision best fits the child's developmental needs?

choices.A: Replace the writing task with drawing or feeling choices followed by a brief child-led story
choices.B: Keep the writing task so the child learns to express grief in an age-independent format
choices.C: Ask the caregiver to write the paragraphs because adult language is more clinically useful

questions.scenarioContext: A 7-year-old receiving counseling after the death of a grandparent has emerging literacy skills. The current plan asks the child to write three paragraphs about emotions each week, but the child engages readily through drawing and storytelling.
questions.explanation: The revision preserves emotional expression while matching the child's literacy level and demonstrated ways of engaging. Retaining an inaccessible task or substituting the caregiver's language would reduce the child's direct participation in treatment.

questions.prompt: Which response best supports care continuity while respecting the client's decision?

choices.A: Contact the specialist with only diagnostic information because limited coordination does not require permission
choices.B: Provide referral details and help the client prepare a concise summary the client may choose to share
choices.C: Withdraw the referral because continuity is possible only when providers communicate with one another

questions.scenarioContext: A client accepts a referral to a pain-management specialist but declines to authorize communication between providers. The client still wants help preparing for the consultation and understands that the counselor cannot coordinate directly without permission.
questions.explanation: The client may pursue the referral without authorizing direct provider communication. Supporting client-mediated information sharing preserves autonomy and continuity, whereas contacting the specialist anyway would disregard the client's stated decision.

questions.prompt: Which assessment approach is most appropriate?

choices.A: Use multiple methods and qualified language support while considering educational opportunity, language development, culture, and measures appropriate for the student's background
choices.B: Use the English test alone because cognitive scores are unaffected by language proficiency or educational experience
choices.C: Delay any assessment indefinitely until the student speaks English without an accent

questions.scenarioContext: A multilingual middle-school student is referred for possible learning difficulties after one year of instruction in English. The school proposes using only an English cognitive test that lacks appropriate norms for students with the learner's language history.
questions.explanation: Assessment should distinguish a possible learning difficulty from language acquisition and unequal educational opportunity using appropriate, multiple sources. An inadequately normed English-only test could produce misleading conclusions, while indefinite delay would also withhold needed evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which assessment plan is most appropriate?

choices.A: Diagnose social anxiety disorder solely because the student now fears negative evaluation
choices.B: Exclude any neurodevelopmental condition because the student was admitted to college
choices.C: Obtain a detailed developmental history and assess both autism-spectrum features and anxiety before determining the formulation

questions.scenarioContext: A college student seeks assessment for social anxiety. The student describes difficulty interpreting social cues since early childhood, intense distress when routines change, longstanding sensory sensitivities, and repeated highly focused interests. Anxiety increased only after peers began criticizing these behaviors.
questions.explanation: Lifelong social-communication differences, restricted interests, sensory sensitivity, and rigidity warrant neurodevelopmental assessment. Current fear of criticism may also support anxiety, so the counselor should evaluate both rather than force an either-or conclusion prematurely.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor or practice do?

choices.A: Apply the credit to future sessions without informing either insurer
choices.B: Correct the coordination error, notify the appropriate parties, and return any overpayment as required
choices.C: Divide the extra payment between the client and the practice because both plans approved the claims

questions.scenarioContext: A billing review shows that both a primary and a secondary insurer paid the full allowed amount for the same sessions because coordination-of-benefits information was entered incorrectly. The resulting credit remains in the client's account.
questions.explanation: Duplicate payment is not earned revenue merely because both claims were processed. Correcting the ledger and resolving the overpayment with the affected payers and client supports accurate billing and prevents improper retention of funds.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Restrict access as needed, report the error, and use the approved process to correct both records while preserving the audit trail
choices.B: Copy the note into Client A's chart and leave the original in place to avoid altering a signed record
choices.C: Permanently delete the misplaced note and avoid reporting it if no one admits reading it

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor discovers that a progress note for Client A was saved in Client B's electronic chart. Clinic policy provides a controlled correction process, requires preservation of the audit trail, and directs staff to assess whether unauthorized access occurred.
questions.explanation: The error affects both record accuracy and possible confidentiality, so it requires controlled correction and review. Silent deletion would erase evidence and bypass assessment, while leaving the note in the wrong chart would perpetuate the clinical risk.

questions.prompt: Which approach provides the most useful evaluation of a counselor's professional strengths and limitations?

choices.A: Rely on confidence because discomfort usually indicates lack of competence
choices.B: Use years of experience as the primary measure because skill increases predictably over time
choices.C: Compare self-reflection with supervision feedback, client-relevant outcomes, and observed performance

questions.explanation: Competence is better evaluated by converging information than by confidence or years in practice. External feedback, performance, and outcomes can reveal strengths or limitations that self-perception alone overlooks.

questions.prompt: Which maintenance plan best strengthens relapse prevention?

choices.A: Remove the transaction blocks gradually to determine whether the client can now gamble in moderation
choices.B: Continue the safeguards and define a same-day support and treatment contact plan for strong urges or any bet
choices.C: Rely on the partner to detect gambling activity before deciding whether additional support is necessary

questions.scenarioContext: A client completing treatment for gambling disorder identifies the start of professional football season as a period of increased urges. The client already uses voluntary self-exclusion, bank transaction blocks, and weekly financial accountability with a trusted partner.
questions.explanation: Existing environmental safeguards reduce access to gambling, and a rapid response plan limits escalation if risk rises or a lapse occurs. Removing protections to test moderation increases exposure to a known seasonal trigger, while relying only on a partner delays the client's own response.

questions.prompt: Which educational step is most appropriate before the counselor recommends whether to use the tool?

choices.A: Learn the vendor's recommended settings because consistent configuration prevents unfair predictions
choices.B: Complete prompt-writing training so the counselor can improve individual risk scores manually
choices.C: Obtain independent education on validation, bias, privacy, human oversight, and effects on the populations served

questions.scenarioContext: A county counseling program asks a counselor to help evaluate an artificial intelligence tool that predicts which clients are likely to miss appointments or deteriorate. The counselor has no training in algorithmic bias or the limits of predictive systems.
questions.explanation: Evaluating a predictive system requires more than operational knowledge because its errors may distribute risks and services unfairly. Independent education on evidence, bias, privacy, and human review prepares the counselor to assess professional implications rather than relying on vendor assurances.

questions.prompt: Which response best demonstrates self-regulation?

choices.A: Pause, notice the defensive reaction, invite the client's perspective, and reflect on the interaction afterward
choices.B: Explain the treatment plan in greater detail so the client can see that the counselor has been attentive
choices.C: End the session early because strong internal reactions make productive discussion impossible

questions.scenarioContext: During a session, a client says that the counselor has not been listening. The counselor's heart rate increases, and the counselor feels an immediate urge to defend the treatment plan and list everything remembered from prior sessions.
questions.explanation: Brief self-regulation enables the counselor to respond to the client's experience rather than act from defensiveness. Explaining harder would bypass the feedback, while ending the session would avoid a potentially useful repair.

questions.prompt: Which intervention should the counselor use?

choices.A: Ask the client to sign a promise that no self-harm will occur before the next session.
choices.B: Identify warning signs, internal coping steps, supportive contacts, professional resources, and ways to reduce access to lethal means.
choices.C: Provide a crisis-line number and instruct the client to use it if the thoughts become more frequent.

questions.scenarioContext: A client reports intermittent suicidal thoughts without current intent or a plan. After a full risk evaluation, the counselor determines that outpatient care with a collaborative safety plan is appropriate under agency procedures. The client is willing to participate.
questions.explanation: A collaborative safety plan provides a sequenced set of personalized actions and supports for managing increased risk. A no-harm promise is not a substitute for intervention, and a crisis-line number alone omits internal coping, social support, and means-safety steps.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Send the summary because the authorization was valid when the client signed it
choices.B: Change the date on the authorization after confirming the client's wishes by telephone
choices.C: Obtain a new valid authorization before releasing the summary

questions.scenarioContext: A client signed an authorization allowing a treatment summary to be sent to a university program. The counselor did not send it before the authorization expired yesterday. Clinic policy requires a current written authorization for this disclosure.
questions.explanation: The authorization no longer permits disclosure after its stated expiration, and clinic policy requires current written permission. Altering the date or relying on the authorization's earlier validity would bypass the client's defined time limit.

questions.prompt: Which action is most appropriate for the counselor?

choices.A: Encourage Nolan to rely on the slight cap-color difference and revisit the issue if an error occurs
choices.B: Suggest taking both medications in the morning so Nolan does not need to identify them later
choices.C: Document the access barrier and help Nolan request verified accessible labeling or packaging through the pharmacy and prescriber

questions.scenarioContext: Nolan has low vision and tells his counselor that he sometimes skips an evening medication because two pharmacy bottles have nearly identical small-print labels. He reports no adverse symptoms. A written authorization permits coordination with the pharmacy and prescriber.
questions.explanation: The problem is reliable access to medication information, not a need for the counselor to change the regimen. Accessible labels or packaging can be verified by the professionals responsible for dispensing and prescribing the medication. Relying on an uncertain visual cue could increase the chance of a medication error.

questions.prompt: Which intervention best supports follow-through?

choices.A: Create an external cue at 7:00 p.m. and rehearse a specific sequence for pausing the game and opening the assignment.
choices.B: Ask the student to rely on motivation and begin whenever the desire to study becomes strong enough.
choices.C: Explore whether procrastination represents unconscious resistance to academic expectations.

questions.scenarioContext: A college student with attention difficulties repeatedly intends to start assignments after dinner but loses track of time while gaming. The student wants a practical strategy and has identified 7:00 p.m. as a realistic start time.
questions.explanation: An external cue and rehearsed transition reduce reliance on time awareness and momentary motivation. The intervention translates the student’s realistic start time into an observable sequence that can be practiced and adjusted.

questions.prompt: Which action best addresses counselor-client fit?

choices.A: Accept the client but avoid discussing any topic related to the lawsuit
choices.B: Ask the client to decide whether the counselor's knowledge of the dispute is a problem
choices.C: Consult appropriately and arrange transfer to the available clinician because the direct conflict may impair objectivity

questions.scenarioContext: At a multisite agency, a counselor is assigned a prospective client who is the plaintiff in an active lawsuit against the counselor's spouse. The counselor has followed the dispute closely, and another qualified clinician is available at a nearby site.
questions.explanation: The counselor's close connection to an active dispute creates a substantial and specific objectivity concern. An available qualified clinician permits continuity without placing the prospective client in the position of evaluating a conflict the counselor already recognizes.

questions.prompt: Which diagnostic assessment is most appropriate?

choices.A: Diagnose a primary schizophrenia-spectrum disorder without examining the timing of substance exposure
choices.B: Clarify the course of symptoms during intoxication, withdrawal, and abstinence before distinguishing a substance-induced condition from a primary psychotic disorder
choices.C: Rule out all psychotic disorders because the client recognizes that methamphetamine can affect perception

questions.scenarioContext: A client reports hearing accusatory voices and feeling watched during periods of methamphetamine use. The symptoms began after heavy use and have repeatedly resolved after sustained abstinence. The client has no known psychotic symptoms before substance use.
questions.explanation: The timing of psychotic symptoms in relation to methamphetamine exposure and resolution during abstinence is central to the differential. Substance involvement does not justify an automatic primary diagnosis or exclusion of all psychotic disorders.

questions.prompt: What is the counselor’s best response?

choices.A: Allow the more fluent partner to interpret because this preserves the couple’s natural communication pattern.
choices.B: Ask the quieter partner to respond only in English so each person’s account can be evaluated consistently.
choices.C: Slow the pace, ask each partner to speak for themself, and explore the quieter partner’s preferred language support.

questions.scenarioContext: In couple counseling, one bilingual partner pauses while searching for words in English. The other partner repeatedly answers on the person’s behalf. The quieter partner looks frustrated but says nothing.
questions.explanation: The counselor protects each partner’s voice and seeks the quieter partner’s own communication preference rather than assuming what support is needed. Letting one partner routinely answer for the other can conceal meaning and reinforce an unequal interaction.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor respond?

choices.A: Explain what the note-taking is for, invite the client’s reaction, and collaborate on an adjustment that supports connection.
choices.B: Stop all note-taking immediately and promise never to write during future sessions.
choices.C: Reassure the client that professional note-taking does not interfere with attentive listening.

questions.scenarioContext: A client says, “You write throughout the whole session. I can’t tell whether you’re listening to me or filling out a form.” The counselor’s notes are brief and can be taken less frequently.
questions.explanation: Transparency and collaborative adjustment respond to the client’s concern without assuming that all documentation must end. Simple reassurance would fail to address the client’s lived experience of disconnection.

questions.prompt: Cronbach's alpha is most commonly used to estimate which characteristic of a multi-item assessment scale?

choices.A: Predictive validity
choices.B: Internal consistency
choices.C: Interrater reliability

questions.explanation: Cronbach's alpha estimates how consistently items on a multi-item scale relate to the same construct. It does not measure agreement between raters or determine how well a score predicts an external outcome.

questions.prompt: Which intervention is most appropriate?

choices.A: Encourage the client to answer every worry with evidence that the feared event cannot occur.
choices.B: Establish a limited scheduled worry period and practice redirecting worry to that period when it appears earlier.
choices.C: Ask the client to avoid all situations that tend to trigger uncertain thoughts.

questions.scenarioContext: A client with persistent worry spends hours each evening mentally reviewing possible problems. Attempts to suppress the thoughts make them return more strongly. The client wants a structured way to reduce the disruption.
questions.explanation: Scheduled worry contains rather than suppresses the process and gives the client a structured response when worries arise. Trying to prove that every feared outcome is impossible can become another form of reassurance and is unrealistic in the face of uncertainty.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Download the charts because the counselor created most of the clinical content
choices.B: Follow the custody and notice requirements and access or transfer records only through authorized processes
choices.C: Delete the charts from the practice system after notifying clients of the departure

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor is leaving a group practice. The employment agreement and applicable law designate the practice as records custodian and require clients to receive notice of continuity options. The counselor wants to download all client charts to a personal drive for future reference.
questions.explanation: Creating clinical content does not give the departing counselor personal ownership of the charts under the stated agreement and law. Authorized custody, notice, and transfer procedures protect continuity and confidentiality without copying or deleting records unilaterally.

questions.prompt: Which response would be most therapeutic?

choices.A: “You’re wondering whether I’m disappointed. What did you notice from me that led you to ask?”
choices.B: “No, counselors are trained not to judge clients for relapses.”
choices.C: “The important issue is how you feel about the relapse, not how I feel about it.”

questions.scenarioContext: After describing a relapse in gambling, a client watches the counselor closely and asks, “Are you disappointed in me?” The counselor does not feel disappointed and is unsure what the client observed.
questions.explanation: The response reflects the client’s concern and invites exploration of the immediate relational cue without defensively denying it. A generic statement about counselor training does not clarify what occurred between this client and counselor.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate response to the counselor's reaction?

choices.A: Describe the counselor's foster-care history and let the client choose which personal help to accept
choices.B: Transfer the client immediately because shared life experience always prevents professional objectivity
choices.C: Examine the rescue impulse in supervision and help the client access appropriate supports without creating personal dependency

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor who previously aged out of foster care is working with a young adult preparing to leave foster care. After hearing about the client's housing uncertainty, the counselor feels a strong urge to provide a personal telephone number, money, and a temporary room at home.
questions.explanation: Shared experience may strengthen empathy, but it can also activate a rescue response that blurs professional roles. Supervision can help the counselor use the awareness constructively while connecting the client with sustainable resources rather than personal aid.

questions.prompt: What does a larger standard error of measurement indicate about an individual test score?

choices.A: The score has stronger content validity
choices.B: The score represents a higher percentile rank
choices.C: The score is estimated with less precision

questions.explanation: The standard error of measurement reflects uncertainty around an observed score. A larger value produces a wider likely range for the person's underlying score and therefore indicates less precision.

questions.prompt: Which information should have the greatest influence when selecting a counseling modality for a treatment plan?

choices.A: The client's needs, preferences, access, relevant evidence, and any contraindications
choices.B: The modality most commonly paired with the client's diagnostic label in agency templates
choices.C: The approach the counselor uses most often, regardless of the client's circumstances

questions.explanation: Modality selection should integrate clinical fit with client preference, feasibility, evidence, and safety. A diagnostic label or counselor habit alone cannot establish that a particular modality is appropriate for an individual client.

questions.prompt: Which coordination action best supports the school transition?

choices.A: Forward the entire school counseling file without discussing which supports Avery wants continued
choices.B: Wait until after the move so the receiving counselor can assess Avery without prior expectations
choices.C: Prepare a concise handoff of effective supports, Avery's preferences, and pending needs, and arrange an introductory contact

questions.scenarioContext: Avery, a high school student in a military family, will move to another state in three weeks. Avery and a parent have authorized coordination with the receiving school counselor. Avery wants continued support for lunchtime anxiety and values being able to visit the counseling office briefly when overwhelmed.
questions.explanation: A focused handoff gives the receiving counselor actionable continuity information and includes Avery's preferences. An introductory contact can reduce the gap created by the move. Forwarding the entire file without selecting relevant content may obscure the supports that matter most.

questions.prompt: What is the counselor's best response?

choices.A: Explain the purpose and sequence of the intake, clarify the client's expectations, and gather sufficient biopsychosocial information before offering a formulation
choices.B: Select a diagnosis from the presenting concern so the client does not feel disappointed
choices.C: Begin a detailed intervention plan without assessing history, functioning, strengths, or risks

questions.scenarioContext: Ten minutes into an initial interview, a client asks the counselor to provide a definitive diagnosis and a detailed treatment plan. Only the presenting concern and basic contact information have been discussed.
questions.explanation: A defensible formulation and plan require enough information about history, functioning, strengths, risks, and goals. Clarifying the process respects the client's request without making a premature diagnosis or beginning an unsupported plan.

questions.prompt: Which initial goal best reflects collaborative prioritization?

choices.A: Establish a shared trial of device-free meals while continuing to assess gaming, friendships, and family conflict
choices.B: Adopt complete gaming abstinence because the caregivers hold responsibility for household rules
choices.C: Focus only on the adolescent's friendship needs because treatment goals must belong to the youngest family member

questions.scenarioContext: In family counseling, two caregivers want their 16-year-old to stop all online gaming. The adolescent wants fewer arguments and says gaming is the main way of maintaining friendships. All agree that meals have become a frequent conflict point.
questions.explanation: The proposed trial begins with a concrete area of agreement and allows the family to gather information about the wider concerns. Adopting either the caregivers' total abstinence demand or only the adolescent's perspective would bypass collaborative family goal setting.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Release the notes because parents always control a minor's counseling information
choices.B: Give the parent a verbal summary because oral disclosure is not a release of records
choices.C: Follow the adolescent-consent law, maintain confidentiality, and discuss permissible family involvement with the client

questions.scenarioContext: A 16-year-old independently consents to counseling under a state law that also gives the adolescent control over disclosure of those records. A parent demands detailed session notes, and no safety exception or court order applies.
questions.explanation: The supplied law gives the adolescent both treatment consent and control of the related disclosure. Parental status alone does not override that rule, and an oral summary would still disclose confidential information.

questions.prompt: What is the counselor's best response?

choices.A: Require the client to finish a complete trauma narrative so the intake record is comprehensive
choices.B: Stop the client from mentioning trauma at any point during the intake
choices.C: Acknowledge the distress, offer to slow the pace, and explain how the structured intake can gather necessary information without requiring a detailed narrative now

questions.scenarioContext: Within minutes of an initial appointment, a client begins describing a traumatic event in graphic detail and becomes visibly overwhelmed. The agency's intake normally starts with current needs, safety, service expectations, and a broad history before detailed trauma exploration.
questions.explanation: The counselor can validate the client's experience and maintain the purpose of intake without encouraging overwhelming exposure. A detailed trauma narrative is not required to establish current needs and safety, but banning all mention of trauma would also be unresponsive.

questions.prompt: What should the counselor do?

choices.A: Leave the listing unchanged because the insurer, not the counselor, published it
choices.B: Request prompt correction and give prospective clients accurate information in the meantime
choices.C: Accept the specialty referrals as long as the clients sign a general informed-consent form

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor discovers that an insurer's online directory lists an outdated office address and a specialty the counselor does not hold. Prospective clients have begun calling for that specialty.
questions.explanation: Counselors share responsibility for addressing material public inaccuracies about their practice once discovered. Accepting referrals under a false specialty or simply blaming the insurer would leave consumers exposed to misleading information.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor respond?

choices.A: Refuse because no information may ever be released after a client's death
choices.B: Release the complete clinical record because an executor automatically needs every counseling detail
choices.C: Verify the documents and provide the records relevant to the authorized estate purpose through a secure process

questions.scenarioContext: A court-appointed executor requests billing records needed to settle a deceased client's estate. The applicable law treats the executor as the client's personal representative for relevant records, and the executor provides valid appointment documents.
questions.explanation: The controlling law gives a verified executor representative authority for relevant records. That authority supports a purpose-limited disclosure, not a categorical refusal or automatic release of every clinical detail.

questions.prompt: Which learning plan would best prepare the counselor to serve this population?

choices.A: Adapt the childhood methods independently because the core features of autism remain the same across age groups
choices.B: Study current adult and autism-affirming evidence, include autistic perspectives, and obtain qualified feedback on practice
choices.C: Continue current methods until an autistic client reports that the approach is ineffective

questions.scenarioContext: An agency is receiving more requests from autistic adults seeking counseling for workplace stress. A counselor's prior education focused almost entirely on childhood deficit models and did not address adult or autism-affirming practice.
questions.explanation: The counselor has identified outdated and incomplete preparation for the population now seeking service. Current evidence, lived perspectives, and feedback support responsive skill development more effectively than unexamined transfer of childhood methods.

questions.prompt: What is the best response?

choices.A: Administer the inventory and note the student's age as a limitation in the report
choices.B: Let the student's parent interpret the results because the parent knows the student's interests
choices.C: Verify population and purpose suitability, consult as needed, and select an appropriate alternative if support is lacking

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor is trained to use an adult career-interest inventory. A middle school asks the counselor to administer it to a 13-year-old to determine eligibility for a technical education track. The counselor has not established that the instrument is appropriate for this age or purpose.
questions.explanation: Assessment competence includes determining whether an instrument is supported for the examinee and the decision being made. Merely noting an unsupported use afterward does not make the resulting interpretation suitable for placement.

questions.prompt: Which feedback is most useful?

choices.A: “You need to project confidence if you want an interviewer to take you seriously.”
choices.B: “Your interview skills will improve after you work through the anxiety underneath them.”
choices.C: “Your answers were clear, and I had difficulty hearing the last two. Would you like to practice them at a stronger volume?”

questions.scenarioContext: A client practicing for a job interview asks for feedback. During rehearsal, the client gives thoughtful answers but speaks so softly that the counselor can barely hear them.
questions.explanation: Constructive feedback is specific, behaviorally observable, balanced, and connected to an immediate opportunity for practice. A global judgment about confidence is less precise and can sound evaluative rather than collaborative.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful next assessment step?

choices.A: Rely on the parent's report because an adolescent's self-report about substance use is inherently invalid
choices.B: Order a comprehensive adult personality inventory before asking additional substance-use questions
choices.C: Explain the limits of privacy, conduct an appropriate private portion of the interview, and combine an adolescent substance-use screen with follow-up questions

questions.scenarioContext: A 16-year-old is referred after a school employee noticed cannabis vaping. A parent remains in the room and answers most substance-use questions. The adolescent gives brief answers and watches the parent before responding.
questions.explanation: A private, developmentally appropriate portion of the assessment can improve disclosure while preserving stated confidentiality limits. A validated adolescent screen should inform, not replace, follow-up questions and information from other relevant sources.

questions.prompt: What should the practice do?

choices.A: Continue using the system because consistent automation is less biased than staff judgment
choices.B: Keep the routing rule but add a notice that insurance type may affect scheduling
choices.C: Suspend the discriminatory routing, review affected applications, and audit and correct the system before reuse

questions.scenarioContext: An automated intake system routes applicants who use public insurance to a waitlist even when clinicians have matching openings. Practice policy prohibits payer-based discrimination and requires human review of consequential automated decisions.
questions.explanation: Automated consistency does not make a discriminatory rule acceptable. Human review, remediation for affected applicants, and correction of the system are necessary before it can again influence access to services.

questions.prompt: What is the leader’s best intervention?

choices.A: Ask the member to prepare written statements before each meeting to keep the discussion moving.
choices.B: Name the pattern, ask the member what would support participation, and invite the group to tolerate a slower pace.
choices.C: Direct the other members to remain completely silent whenever this member begins speaking.

questions.scenarioContext: In a counseling group, one member says, “I need extra time to put my thoughts into words.” Other members often finish the member’s sentences or move on during pauses. The member has begun participating less.
questions.explanation: This intervention protects the member’s opportunity to participate while inviting the member’s own preferences and making the group process visible. Requiring prepared statements shifts the burden entirely to the member, while total silence from others imposes an inflexible rule without collaboration.

questions.prompt: When a client and counselor revise a treatment goal, which documentation best supports continuity of care?

choices.A: Replace the original goal with the new goal so later readers see only the current plan
choices.B: Record the change, the client's reason for it, the revised goal, and the related next step
choices.C: Retain the original goal without revision until the client's diagnosis also changes

questions.explanation: This documentation preserves the treatment history while making the current direction and client involvement clear. Replacing the old goal without context obscures how the plan evolved. A goal can change without a diagnostic change.

questions.prompt: What should the clinic do?

choices.A: Leave the backup in place because restoration testing proved that it works
choices.B: Download another copy to a personal drive before anyone changes the account
choices.C: Secure the repository, report and assess the exposure, and migrate backups to approved encrypted storage

questions.scenarioContext: During a restoration drill, a clinic learns that its backup service has copied unencrypted counseling records into an unapproved consumer cloud account. Security policy requires encrypted backups in approved storage and immediate review of unauthorized repositories.
questions.explanation: A working backup is not compliant when it is unencrypted and stored in an unauthorized location. The clinic must contain and assess the exposure, then restore a backup process that meets the stated security requirements.

questions.prompt: How is unconditional positive regard best expressed when a client describes behavior that harmed another person?

choices.A: Maintain respect for the client while openly exploring the behavior, its effects, and responsibility for change.
choices.B: Avoid discussing the harm so the client does not experience the counselor as judgmental.
choices.C: Communicate approval of the behavior to demonstrate complete acceptance of the client.

questions.explanation: Unconditional positive regard concerns the client’s worth as a person, not approval of every action. The counselor can maintain acceptance while addressing harm honestly and supporting accountability.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate plan revision?

choices.A: Retain the transition goal because it may eventually reduce anxiety even if the client is uncertain
choices.B: Remove the presumed goal and collaborate on the client's anxiety priorities, exploring identity only as the client wishes
choices.C: Replace the transition goal with an objective to decide on a transition before anxiety treatment begins

questions.scenarioContext: A transgender client seeks counseling for anxiety and says they are undecided about any social transition. A draft plan written by a previous provider lists beginning a social transition as a treatment goal, but the client does not identify that as an objective.
questions.explanation: Treatment goals should reflect the client's stated needs rather than an assumed course of gender expression. The counselor can remain open to identity exploration without making a transition decision a prerequisite for anxiety care.

questions.prompt: How should the counselor respond?

choices.A: Remind the client of the agreement and coach the client to notice anxiety without resolving the uncertainty.
choices.B: Reassure the client once so anxiety falls enough to complete the exposure.
choices.C: End the exposure because the reassurance requests show that the client is not ready for this method.

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor trained in exposure and response prevention is guiding a planned contamination exposure. The client asks repeatedly, “You know I won’t get sick from touching this, right?” The client and counselor previously agreed that seeking reassurance maintains the fear cycle.
questions.explanation: Response prevention requires interrupting reassurance seeking while helping the client remain in contact with uncertainty and anxiety. Providing reassurance would offer short-term relief but reinforce the cycle that the planned intervention is intended to change.

questions.prompt: What is the best next professional development step?

choices.A: Review current research and professional guidance, clarify training standards and scope, and seek qualified instruction before representing competence
choices.B: Purchase the equipment and practice with selected clients while completing self-paced tutorials
choices.C: Adopt the method for concerns described in colleague testimonials because peer experience is practice-based evidence

questions.scenarioContext: A counselor is considering adding neurofeedback after hearing enthusiastic reports from colleagues. The counselor has no training in the method and finds mixed claims about its uses and evidence base.
questions.explanation: Mixed claims and lack of training call for a deliberate evaluation of evidence, scope, and preparation requirements. Colleague enthusiasm, equipment ownership, and tutorials do not by themselves establish competence or appropriate use.

questions.prompt: Which use of case conceptualization contributes most directly to treatment planning?

choices.A: Compiling a complete chronological history without forming conclusions about what maintains the concern
choices.B: Selecting interventions from the diagnostic label without considering current protective factors
choices.C: Organizing contributing and protective factors into testable hypotheses that guide goals and interventions

questions.explanation: A useful conceptualization explains how relevant factors may contribute to or protect against the current problem and connects those hypotheses to the plan. A chronology or diagnosis without such integration provides less individualized direction.

questions.prompt: Which objective best makes the goal measurable and attainable?

choices.A: The partners will eliminate all disagreements during daily check-ins for four weeks
choices.B: The partners will complete a 10-minute check-in four evenings weekly and track escalation for four weeks
choices.C: The partners will hold check-ins when needed and discuss progress at the next four sessions

questions.scenarioContext: Two partners identify “communicate better” as a counseling goal. They currently have about five escalating arguments each week and agree that a short evening check-in is feasible.
questions.explanation: This objective specifies an observable shared behavior, frequency, duration, monitoring method, and time frame that the partners consider feasible. Eliminating all disagreement is unrealistic, whereas holding check-ins only “when needed” is insufficiently measurable.

questions.prompt: Which outcome best demonstrates that a referral loop has been closed?

choices.A: The receiving service has the needed authorized information, responsibilities are clear, and the client has connected with care
choices.B: The counselor has sent a referral form and documented the date, even though receipt has not been confirmed
choices.C: The client has received several provider names and understands that arranging care is now solely the client's responsibility
